challenges.name: graceful-degradation-quiz
challenges.title: What should a Redis outage cost the progress path?
challenges.description: Two pieces of evidence from the Redis outage: the trace of one failed progress update, and the retry queue of a first fix that replayed an old score.

questions.question:
Trace of one POST /progress during the Redis outage, before the fix (the Redis client had no command timeout set and gave up after 5 s):

POST /progress                                  5,031 ms  503
  pg: INSERT lesson_progress ... COMMIT            14 ms  ok
  redis: DEL progress:u_51                      5,000 ms  ERR connection timeout
  (leaderboard ZADD not reached)

The fix: a 50 ms timeout on every Redis call, a circuit breaker per Redis dependency (cache, leaderboard) that opens after 3 consecutive failures, the leaderboard update moved to a retry queue on failure, and a cache failure no longer fails the request.

Statement: "With the fix, this request returns 200 with degraded: true after about 114 ms (14 + 50 + 50), and once both breakers are open the same request takes about 14 ms."
questions.explanation: True. The progress row is committed in PostgreSQL in 14 ms; that is the part that must succeed. Each Redis call can now cost at most its 50 ms timeout, so while the breakers are still closed a request pays 14 + 50 (cache) + 50 (leaderboard) = 114 ms and answers 200 with degraded: true and the leaderboard update queued. After 3 consecutive failures each breaker opens and calls are skipped without waiting, so the request costs only the PostgreSQL write. The common misconception is that a timeout alone is enough: without a breaker every request still pays the full timeout of every dead dependency, and under load those waits hold connections and workers for the whole outage.

False. Idempotent means applying the same write twice gives the same result as once; it says nothing about order. The queued write carries the total from 10:00:01 (120) and runs after a newer direct write (150), so the leaderboard ends at 120 and stays wrong until the learner's next update. Queue the user id instead and read the current total from PostgreSQL when draining, or remove the user from the queue when a direct write succeeds, or use versioned scores that refuse older values (Redis Patterns, "Apply only newer events"). The misconception is that an idempotent write is automatically safe to retry later; a delayed retry is also a reordered write.

challenges.name: progress-graceful-degradation
challenges.title: Progress that survives a Redis outage: timeouts, breakers and a retry queue
challenges.description: A Redis outage made every POST /progress fail with 503 after 5 s, although the progress row was already committed in PostgreSQL. Implement class CircuitBreaker and class ProgressService(deps, config) on a fake clock; the infrastructure fakes (ProgressStore = PostgreSQL, Cache and Leaderboard = Redis, with scripted outages) are given. Calling "cache" or "leaderboard" (config[name] = { timeoutMs, failureThreshold, openMs }): ask its breaker; not allowed -> skipped, 0 ms. Otherwise call: ok and latencyMs <= timeoutMs is a success taking latencyMs; ok false is a failure taking min(latencyMs, timeoutMs); ok but slower than timeoutMs is a timeout, a failure taking timeoutMs. Breaker: closed allows every call, a success resets the consecutive failures, failureThreshold consecutive failures open it at that now; open allows nothing until now >= openedAt + openMs, from then on state(now) is "half-open" and one trial call goes through: success closes it (failures 0), failure opens it again at that now. updateProgress({ userId, lessonId, points }, now): 400 { total: null, degraded: false, skipped: [], latencyMs: 0 } unless userId and lessonId are non-empty strings and points is an integer 0-1000 (nothing called). Otherwise store.complete(...) -> { total, latencyMs }; cache.invalidate("progress:<userId>") (not a success -> skipped "cache"); leaderboard.setScore(userId, total): success removes userId from the retry queue, anything else adds skipped "leaderboard" and appends userId unless already queued. Return 200 { total, degraded: skipped not empty, skipped, latencyMs: sum of all call times }. drain(now): up to drainBatch users: ask the leaderboard breaker (stop if not allowed), setScore(first user, store.total(user)) - the total read now; success removes it, failure stops. Return the count written. getLeaderboard(n, now): leaderboard.top(n) success -> source "redis", rows from Redis; otherwise source "postgres", rows = store.top(n). degraded = rows from PostgreSQL or retry queue not empty; latencyMs = Redis call time + PostgreSQL query time (if made). pending() = queued user ids in order; breakerState(name, now). Input: { config: { cache, leaderboard, drainBatch }, outages: { cache?, leaderboard? }, drainEveryMs, untilMs, events: [{ at, type: "progress", userId, lessonId, points } | { at, type: "top", n }] }. The runner prints final breaker states, the retry queue, the users the leaderboard is behind on, call counts, degraded count, total latency, breaker transitions and one line per request and drain.
hints: Which single step of a progress update must succeed for the learner's work to be safe, and what is the most each of the other steps may cost the request when its dependency is slow, failing, or known to be down?

Write one private helper that every Redis call goes through: it asks the breaker, makes the call, classifies the outcome (success, failure, timeout) with the dependency's own timeoutMs, reports it to the breaker, and returns whether it succeeded and how many milliseconds it cost. Then look at the retry queue twice: what is stored in it (a user id, not a score) and what removes a user from it (a successful direct write or a successful drain).

A worked trace with failureThreshold 2, openMs 1,000 and timeoutMs 50, for a dependency that is slow (300 ms) from 0 to 1,500: call at 0 -> timeout, 50 ms, 1 failure. Call at 10 -> timeout, 50 ms, breaker opens at 10. Call at 500 -> skipped, 0 ms (state open). Call at 1,010 -> state half-open, trial call -> timeout, 50 ms, opens again at 1,010. Call at 1,500 -> skipped. Call at 2,010 -> trial call succeeds in 2 ms, breaker closed, failures 0. For a user queued at 10 with total 40 who completes another lesson at 500 (total 70, still failing), a drain after 2,010 must write 70.
